question: Can you keep following one theme when another begins above or below it?
intro: Four plain notes open a finale of astonishing contrapuntal invention. Mozart lets the themes behave like characters in a fast-moving conversation, then brings several of them together in the closing stretch. Bruno Walter conducts the Columbia Symphony Orchestra.

sections.label: Exposition · the ideas meet
sections.mNote: C major moves towards the dominant, G

sections.label: Development · themes in motion
sections.mNote: Imitation and sequence unsettle the tonal ground

sections.label: Recapitulation · the tonic returns
sections.mNote: Earlier material returns in the home-key argument

sections.label: Coda · the ideas combine
sections.mNote: Contrapuntal combinations lead to the final C-major close

cues.title: Four notes, many possibilities
cues.text: The first violins begin with four long notes: C–D–F–E. Their plain shape makes them easy to recognise when Mozart moves them between instruments, changes their direction, or sets quicker material against them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1880), finale, PDF p. 35, bars 1–8; report begins quietly in C major. The pitch sequence and first-violin scoring are read directly from the score.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow a line underneath
cues.text: Do not listen only to the highest or loudest part. The finale repeatedly lets one idea continue while another starts elsewhere; try keeping your attention on a line after the foreground changes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, opening contrapuntal passages, PDF pp. 36–38; report strong early span followed by lower relative level around 0:40. This is a general listening task rather than an exact entry marker.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Contrasting ideas belong together
cues.text: Quicker figures and more smoothly shaped phrases provide contrast with the opening four notes. The opposition is not simply melody against accompaniment: these materials are capable of changing places and working together.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, exposition, PDF pp. 38–40; report moves through a D-centred passage around 1:00–1:10 before the more sustained dominant region. The guide does not identify a new theme from the key estimator alone.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A remarkable summer
cues.text: Mozart completes his last three symphonies during the summer of 1788. The Jupiter is entered in his catalogue on 10 August. The surviving chronology is clearer than the evidence for any performance he heard.
cues.evidence: Mozart composer biography; K. Dawn Grapes, Fort Collins Symphony programme note, “Mozart Symphony No. 41”, https://fcsymphony.org/mozart-41-jupiter/.

cues.title: Cadences do not end the motion
cues.text: The exposition presses towards a close in G major. Listen for how running figures and exchanges between parts can keep the surface moving even while the harmony makes its destination clear.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, bars 138–157, PDF pp. 42–43; report is strongly G-major centred across 2:10–2:30 before a quieter span at 2:35–2:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The themes leave safe ground
cues.text: The development carries recognisable material through less settled harmony. Sequence means repeating a shape at a different pitch; imitation means one part taking up what another has begun. Here both can contribute to the sense of movement.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, development beginning bar 158, PDF pp. 43–46; report boundary 2:48 followed by changing pitch profiles and stronger 2:55–3:05 windows.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Changing positions, familiar shapes
cues.text: The development makes the listener work to separate the lines. Hear the parts as simultaneous melodies rather than as a single block of sound: the same small shapes can occupy different registers and harmonic surroundings.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, bars 199–224, PDF pp. 45–46; report boundaries 3:32 and 3:46 bracket the later developmental passage and return preparation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return without simplification
cues.text: The home-key return does not cancel the finale’s contrapuntal habits. The opening material comes back into the C-major argument, but its lines continue to overlap and exchange roles.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, recapitulation from bar 225, PDF pp. 46–48; report strongest boundary 3:46, followed by C-centred windows and renewed higher relative level. The 3:46 marker is provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The nickname comes later
cues.text: Mozart does not call this symphony Jupiter. The later nickname offers a useful handle, but it is not a programme supplied by the composer, and it should not dictate a story for the music.
cues.evidence: K. Dawn Grapes, Fort Collins Symphony programme note, “Mozart Symphony No. 41”, https://fcsymphony.org/mozart-41-jupiter/.

cues.title: Hear the separate layers
cues.text: Choose one short figure and follow it through the texture. If you lose it, listen for its rhythm rather than its exact pitch; Mozart can preserve a musical identity while moving it to a different place.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, recapitulation, PDF pp. 50–52; report shows a sustained, relatively strong C-major region across 5:00–5:50. This listening task does not claim an isolated entry.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Debt is not a programme
cues.text: Mozart’s letters to Michael Puchberg document requests for loans in 1788. Those circumstances belong to the work’s history, but they do not explain each modulation or tell us what a particular theme must mean.
cues.evidence: Mozart composer biography, Vienna and the late 1780s; financial evidence is distinguished from a musical programme.

cues.title: Several ideas at once
cues.text: The coda brings five thematic ideas into contrapuntal combinations. Listen for independence inside the crowded texture: a sustained line, a quick figure and a rhythmic answer can remain distinct even while they support one another.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, bars 372–404, PDF pp. 54–55; report boundary 6:20 and stronger 6:20–6:40 windows. The five-theme combination is score-derived; no exact simultaneous entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Complexity becomes a clear ending
cues.text: The final orchestral statements make C major unmistakable. After so much movement between independent lines, the decisive closing gestures sound like a shared conclusion rather than a gradual thinning away.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf finale, bars 405–424, PDF p. 56; report strong 6:55–7:05 windows followed by much lower relative level at 7:10–7:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A quiet close becomes a new beginning
transitions.how: The exposition closes in the dominant, G major. A quieter texture then reuses familiar material as a starting point for harmonic travel. Motives link the sections, while sequence and imitation change their purpose: the themes are no longer being introduced but tested in new surroundings.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf finale, bars 151–169, PDF pp. 43–44; report lower-level 2:35–2:45 span and novelty boundary 2:48. The 2:34 marker estimates the start of the developmental paragraph.

transitions.title: The bass prepares the homecoming
transitions.how: The development’s travelling counterpoint gives way to preparation for C major. The four-note opening idea returns above moving inner strings, making the homecoming audible as a relationship between lines rather than a completely new texture. The reprise will resolve the exposition’s material into the tonic.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf finale, bars 219–233, PDF pp. 46–47: dominant preparation and main-theme return at bar 225. Report boundary 3:46 and C-centred window at 3:50 support a provisional 3:46 marker.

transitions.title: A cadence releases the final combination
transitions.how: The recapitulatory close reaches C major, but Mozart continues beyond it. A strong gesture yields to quieter sustained notes and an inverted version of the four-note idea. From this reduced texture the coda builds its combinations, allowing several established themes to act together before the final cadences.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf finale, bars 355–383, PDF p. 54: coda from bar 357, quieter inversion from bar 361, contrapuntal build from bar 372. Report reduction near 6:05–6:15 and boundary 6:20; coda marker 5:58 is score-proportion, not a detected attack.

timeline.note: Four-note first-violin theme over moving second violins; further strings join as the phrase expands.
The full orchestra reinforces the opening paragraph, including trumpets and timpani.
The development begins in a reduced string texture with held horn support; woodwinds rejoin within the paragraph. This is an approximate passage state, not continuous activity.
Woodwinds and strings share the travelling contrapuntal material, with intermittent horn, trumpet and timpani punctuation. Activity changes within this approximate passage.

The opening theme returns over moving inner strings; winds, horns, trumpets and timpani support the returning phrase intermittently. This passage state is not an exact entrance or continuous-tutti map.
The reprise includes full-orchestral statements as well as reduced counterpoint.
A strong orchestral gesture opens the coda before the texture contracts.
Sustained lines expose the inverted four-note idea; the low-string division is not separately staged.
The contrapuntal combination expands towards the final tutti; this is a passage ensemble, not a claim that every part sounds continuously.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
